text: Lithium-Sulfur Batteries Very Important Paper Improving Rate Performance of Encapsulating Lithium-Polysulfide Electrolytes for Practical Lithium� Sulfur Batteries Li-Ling Su, Nan Yao, Zheng Li, Chen-Xi Bi, Zi-Xian Chen, Xiang Chen, Bo-Quan Li, Xue-Qiang Zhang,* and Jia-Qi Huang* Abstract: The cycle life of high-energy-density lithium� sulfur (Li� S) batteries is severely plagued by the incessant parasitic reactions between Li metal anodes and reactive Li polysulfides (LiPSs).
Encapsulating Li-polysulfide electrolyte (EPSE) emerges as an effective electrolyte design to mitigate the parasitic reactions kinetically.
Nevertheless, the rate performance of Li� S batteries with EPSE is synchronously suppressed.
Herein, the sacrifice in rate performance by EPSE is circumvented while mitigating parasitic reactions by employing hexyl methyl ether (HME) as a cosolvent.
The specific capacity of Li� S batteries with HME-based EPSE is nearly not decreased at 0.1 C compared with conventional ether electrolytes.

With an ultrathin Li metal anode (50 μm) and a high-arealloading sulfur cathode (4.4 mgScm� 2), a longer cycle life of 113 cycles was achieved in HME-based EPSE compared with that of 65 cycles in conventional ether electrolytes at 0.1 C.
Furthermore, both high energy density of 387 Whkg� 1 and stable cycle life of 27 cycles were achieved in a Li� S pouch cell (2.7 Ah).
This work inspires the feasibility of regulating the solvation structure of LiPSs in EPSE for Li� S batteries with balanced performance.

Introduction Electrification emerges as a promising strategy for decarburization in the pursuit of net-zero emissions.[1] The development of high-energy-density application areas, such as longendurance unmanned aerial vehicles, urgently requires advanced high-energy-density rechargeable batteries.[2] Lithium� sulfur (Li� S) battery with an ultrahigh theoretical energy density of 2600 Whkg� 1 is regarded as a promising next-generation battery candidate.[3] Li� S batteries with energy density over 500 Whkg� 1 at the cell level have been realized.[3d] However, the practical applications of Li� S batteries are still plagued by their poor cycle life under demanding conditions including a high-loading S cathode (> 6.0 mgScm� 2), a low electrolyte/sulfur (E/S) ratio (< 3.0 μLmgS � 1), and a limited Li metal inventory (<100 μm).[4] The short cycle life of Li� S batteries mainly results from the rapid depletion of lean electrolytes and limited active Li.[4a,5] Concretely, massive soluble Li polysulfides (LiPSs) are generated in the S cathode to enable typical solid� liquid� solid conversion reactions and provide high discharge-specific-capacity over 1000 mAhg� 1 due to rapid charge transfer and redox mediation.[6] However, LiPSs can diffuse to the anode side through a concentration gradient and induce severe parasitic reactions with Li metal anodes, which further results in the notorious shuttle effect.[7] The parasitic reactions deplete active Li inventory, active LiPSs, and electrolytes, finally leading to rapid battery failure.[8] Under mild conditions with an excessive Li inventory (thickness>500 μm), flooded electrolytes (E/S ratio> 15 μLmgS � 1), and a low-loading S cathode (<2.0 mgScm� 2), Li� S batteries can generally deliver stable cycle performance owing to much excessive Li inventory despite the existence of the parasitic reactions.[9] However, under demanding conditions as mentioned above, meager active materials are rapidly depleted, severely shortening the cycle life of practical Li� S batteries.[10] The solvation structure of LiPSs plays a vital role in dictating the reaction kinetics with Li metal anodes as reported.[11] Therefore, regulating the solvation structure of LiPSs emerges as a promising strategy to improve the cycle performance of Li� S batteries.

Encapsulating Li-polysulfide electrolyte (EPSE) was proposed to inhibit the parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li metal anodes, where LiPSs are encapsulated by a bilayer solvation shell.[12] With strong-solvating-power solvents in the inner layer, such as 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME), the solid� liquid� solid conversion reactions of S cathode are allowed.[13] The outer shell solvents with weak [*] L.-L.

solvating power and superior reduction stability to Li metal impair the reactivity of LiPSs with Li metal anodes kinetically, such as di-isopropyl sulfide (DIPS), isopropyl ether (DIPE), and 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl-2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (HFE).[12,14] Although available EPSEs attempt to maintain smooth conversion reactions of S cathode furthest, adverse effects are inevitable for S conversion reaction kinetics, especially at high working rat es.[12,14–15] Specifically, the specific capacity of S cathodes in current EPSEs decreases by over 50 mAhg� 1, and the polarization at the second discharge plateau increases by 0.05–0.2 V at working rates around 0.1 C.

Therefore, a refined design of the solvation structure of LiPSs in EPSE is imperative to circumvent the suppression in conversion reaction kinetics of S cathode while impairing parasitic reactions kinetics of LiPSs with Li metal anodes.
Herein, hexyl methyl ether (HME) is proposed as an outer shell solvent to construct HME-based EPSE (HME- EPSE) to balance the rate and cycle performance of practical Li� S batteries.
The solvation structure of LiPSs in HME-EPSE is characterized by molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, resembling that in other EPSEs.

With HME- EPSE, the specific capacity of Li� S batteries is 1040 mAhg� 1 at the working rate of 0.1 C, which is nearly equal to that in conventional ether electrolytes, implying that the conversion reaction kinetics of S cathode is almost preserved.

Meanwhile, a prolonged cycle life from 65 to 113 cycles is achieved using HME-EPSE under demanding conditions including an ultrathin Li metal anode (50 μm) and a highareal-loading sulfur cathode (4.4 mgScm� 2).
The prolonged cycle life originates from the suppressed parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li metal anodes.
Furthermore, a 2.7 Ahpouch cell with HME-EPSE undergoes 27 cycles with a high initial energy density of 387 Whkg� 1 .

Results and Discussion Solvation structure of LiPSs in HME-EPSE The weak solvating power and high reduction stability toward Li metal are two basic conditions of the outer solvent in EPSE to regulate the solvation structure of LiPSs.
HME has a long carbon chain (� C6H13) on one side of the oxygen atom, resulting in a large steric hindrance for the coordination of O atom.[14,16] Thus, the poor solvating power of HME is expected.
Moreover, the stability of HME (pure solvent) towards Li metal is evaluated by the cyclic voltammetry (CV) test.
Considering that the reduction reactions of the solvent mainly occur at less than 2.00 V vs.
Li/Li+, the voltage scan range is set as 0–2.00 V with a scanning rate of 0.5 mVs� 1.
At about 0.01 V, the reduction peak currents of DOL and DME are 6.700 and 15.500 μAcm� 2, respectively (Figure S1).
In contrast, the reduction current of HME is within 0.017 μAcm� 2, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of DOL and DME.
There is no reduction peak throughout the voltage scan range with HME, indicating a high reduction stability against Li metal.
Therefore, HME meets the two basic conditions to construct EPSE and thus is used to formulate HME-EPSE (DOL/DME/HME= 37.5/37.5/25, by vol.).

The conventional DOL/DME electrolyte (1:1, by vol.) is adopted as the control sample, which is one of the most commonly used ether-based electrolytes in Li� S batteries.[17] 1.0 M bis-(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI) and 2.0 wt% LiNO3 are added in both electrolytes as Li salts and additives, respectively.[18] The solvation structure of LiPSs in HME-EPSE is further unveiled by MD simulations (Figure 1). 0.25 M Li2S8 is employed to better observe the intrinsic solvation structure of LiPSs.[11a,12,14] In DOL/DME electrolyte (Figure 1a and Figure S2), there are two solvent shells according to the distribution position of the solvents.
DOL and DME appear at 3.2 and 2.0 Å, respectively, forming the inner solvent shell (shell 1).
Meanwhile, DOL at 7.0 Å together with DME at 8.5 Å constitute the outer solvent shell (shell 2).

The snapshots and spatial distribution functions (SDFs) around S8 2�in DOL/DME electrolyte provide a concrete view of the solvation structure, which demonstrate the homogeneous inner and outer solvent shells of LiPSs in DOL/DME electrolyte (Figure 1c and 1e).
In HME-EPSE (Figure 1b), the inner solvent shell is still composed of DME (at 2.0 Å) and DOL (at 3.3 Å), which ensures the dissolution Figure 1.

The results of coordination number of the corresponding species coincide well with the results of radial distribution function (Figure S3).
The visualized solvation structures around S8 2�in HME-EPSE also demonstrate that HME distributes in the outer solvent shell (Figure 1d and 1f).
Therefore, the nano-heterogeneous solvation structure of LiPSs in HME- EPSE is confirmed, which resembles the basic features of LiPSs in other EPSEs.
Rate performance of HME-EPSE The rate performance of Li� S batteries under practical conditions with various EPSEs was evaluated despite the similar solvation structure of LiPSs.

An ultrathin Li metal anode (50 μm), a high-loading S cathode of 4.4 mgScm� 2, and an E/S ratio of 6.6 μLmgS � 1 were selected for practical considerations.[4b,20] Li� S batteries were cycled at various rates of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 C (1 C=1672 mAg� 1).
At 0.1 C, Li� S batteries with DOL/DME electrolyte or HME-EPSE deliver similar specific capacities, 1049 and 1040 mAhg� 1, respectively (Figure 2a, 2c).
Furthermore, both electrolytes demonstrate typical two discharge plateaus,[6a,21] implying that HME-EPSE does not affect the conversion behavior of the S cathodes.

and 0.3 C, the battery using HME-EPSE can cycle stably (Figure S4) and delivers a specific capacity of 919 and 869 mAhg� 1, respectively, which is only 2% and 5% lower than that with DOL/DME electrolyte of 942 and 915 mAhg� 1 (Figure 2a and 2e).
The charge� discharge profiles of the batteries at different rates are provided in Figure S5.
Thus, HME-EPSE scarcely sacrifices the specific capacity of the S cathodes at 0.1 to 0.3 C compared with DOL/DME electrolyte.
Furthermore, the rate performance of other EPSEs was also tested (Figure 2b).
In particular, the ratio of DOL, DME, and the outer shell solvent in other EPSEs is the same as HME-EPSE for a fair comparison.
At 0.1 C, the specific capacity is 1040, 948, 929, and 753 mAhg� 1, corresponding to HME, DIPS, HFE, and DIPE-EPSE (Figure 2d).

When current density is increased to 0.2 C, the specific capacity of Li� S batteries with HFE-EPSE and DIPE-EPSE drops sharply to less than 800 mAhg� 1 due to large polarization at the beginning of the second discharge plateau (Figure 2b, 2f, and Figure S6b, S6c).

At 0.3 C, this dramatically increased polarization results in total loss of the second discharge plateau and an extremely low specific capacity of Li� S batteries with HFE-EPSE and DIPE-EPSE (<200 mAhg� 1).

The specific capacity of Li� S batteries with DIPS-EPSE are only 948, 840, and 777 mAhg� 1 at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 C, respectively, which is 10%, 11%, and 15% lower than that cycled in DOL/DME electrolyte (Figure S6a).
Moreover, its second discharge plateau presents a rather high polarization, which is similar to that cycled in HFE-EPSE and DIPE-EPSE.

Specifically, the Li2S nucleation kinetics, corresponding to the potential difference between the nucleation point and the potential plateau (denoted as ΔE, Figure S7), is quantitively compared to reflect the polarization change at the beginning of the second discharge plateau.
From 0.1 to 0.3 C, the ΔE of HME-EPSE ranges from 24.5 to 75.7 mV.

As the current density increases from 0.1 to 0.2 C, the ΔE of DIPS-EPSE, HFE-EPSE, and DIPE- EPSE significantly increases from 43.5 to 97.7 mV, from 101.3 to 284.8 mV, and from 155.6 to 237.7 mV, respectively, demonstrating the cathode kinetics is severely suppressed.
When it comes to 0.3 C, ΔE of DIPS-EPSE further rises to 172.4 mV, more than twice that of the HME-EPSE.
While for the batteries with HFE-EPSE and DIPE-EPSE, the second discharge plateau disappears at 0.3 C, resulting from ΔE being too large to afford a measurable value.
In short, HME-EPSE demonstrates superior rate performance among various EPSEs and delivers similar specific capacity compared with DOL/DME electrolyte within 0.3 C.
Impairing parasitic reactions of LiPSs The effectiveness of HME-EPSE in impairing the parasitic reactions between LiPSs and Li metal anodes was verified in Li� S batteries.

Shuttle current tests were conducted to measure the shuttle effect of LiPSs in DOL/DME electrolyte and HME-EPSE without LiNO3 in electrolytes.[22] HME-EPSE decreases the shuttle current to 0.055 mAcm� 2 when it reaches its peak at 2.35 V, which is reduced by 55% compared with the battery with DOL/DME electrolyte with a peak current of 0.122 mAcm� 2 (Figure 3a), illustrating that the shuttle effect of LiPSs is well mitigated in HME-EPSE.

As the parasitic reactions of LiPSs and Li metal contribute to the formation of S-contained components in solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), the mitigated reaction rate was further proved by analyzing the S-contained components in SEI probed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).[5b,7b] The S atomic content in SEI decreases on the Li metal anode that is cycled in HME-EPSE compared with that in DOL/DME electrolyte although the S-containing species are similar, mainly including Li2S, Li2S2, SO4 2� , and SO3 2�(Figure S8).

At the 5th cycle, the S atomic content on Li metal anodes decreases to 3.1%, 3.9%, 4.0%, and 4.2% (at 0, 40, 80, and 120 s sputtering, respectively) in HME-EPSE, compared with 4.1%, 4.5%, 4.3%, and 4.3% in DOL/DME electrolyte correspondingly (Figure 3b).
At the 50th cycle, the lower S atomic content on Li anodes in HME-EPSE compared with DOL/DME electrolyte is also observed (Figure S9).

When it comes to the cycle performance, coin cells under mild conditions including a low-loading S cathode of 1.1 mgScm� 2, a thick Li metal anode of 600 μm, and flooded electrolytes of E/S ratio >15 μLmgS � 1 were firstly tested (Figure S10).
The cycle life of the battery with HME-EPSE increases to 280 cycles when the capacity decays to 60% of the initial capacity, which is more than twice of DOL/DME electrolyte.
Meanwhile, the Li� S battery using HME-EPSE delivers an initial specific capacity of 856 mAhg� 1, which is comparable to that in DOL/DME electrolyte.

After 100 cycles, the Li� S battery with HME-EPSE exhibits a similar impedance as the battery with DOL/DME electrolyte (13.3 and 14.2 Ω, respectively, Figure S11), indicating a slight reduction in the accumulation of inactive Li caused by the parasitic reactions.[23] To simulate practical circumstances, the cycle performance of coin cells is evaluated under demanding conditions including a high-loading S cathode (4.4 mgScm� 2), an ultrathin Li anode (50 μm), and an E/S ratio of 6.6 μLmgS � 1 (Figure 3c and Figure S12).
The cycle rate was set as 0.1 C.
The cycle life of Li� S battery using HME-EPSE increases to 113 cycles, which is nearly twice that of 65 cycles with DOL/DME electrolyte.
During the early cycles, the charge� discharge profiles of Li� S batteries with DOL/DME electrolyte and HME-EPSE were similar (Figure S13).
Li� S batteries with DOL/DME electrolyte or HME-EPSE exhibit an initial specific capacity of approximately 1010 mAhg� 1.
However, the battery with DOL/DME electrolyte is overcharged at the 65th cycle and then decays rapidly to 652 mAhg� 1 at the 69th cycle due to fast consumption of active Li and electrolytes.
In contrast, at the 69th cycle, the Li� S battery with HME-EPSE maintains a specific capacity of 860 mAhg� 1 with 85% capacity retention and a Coulombic efficiency of 95% (Figure S13).
In addition, a superhigh-loading S cathode of 9.9 mgScm� 2 was employed to confirm the effect of HME-EPSE.
The batteries with HME-EPSE or DOL/DME electrolyte are both activated at 0.05 C for 2 cycles and then cycles at 0.1 C.
At 0.1 C, the initial specific capacity of the battery with HME-EPSE is 737 mAhg� 1, which is lower than that with DOL/DME electrolyte (826 mAhg� 1).

However, after 40 cycles, the battery with HME-EPSE maintains a specific capacity of 482 mAhg� 1 with 65% capacity retention and has far exceeded the battery with DOL/DME electrolyte which delivers 168 mAhg� 1 with only 20% capacity retention (Figure S14).

The morphology of Li deposition after cycles was also recorded by scanning electron microscope (SEM).[5b] The deposited Li in DOL/DME electrolyte and HME-EPSE is both dense at the 5th cycle (Figure S15).
However, at the 50th cycle, the deposited Li in DOL/DME electrolyte becomes porous (Figure 3d).
In contrast, compact Li deposition morphology is still obtained in HME-EPSE (Figure 3e).
Moreover, non-uniform Li deposition and large-area copper collector exposure are macroscopic on the anode after 50 cycles in DOL/DME electrolyte (Figure S16).
The cycled Li metal anode in the battery with HME-EPSE is denser and more uniform, which results from the mitigated reactions between LiPSs and Li metal anodes.
The notable increase in cycle life and residual active Li in Li� S batteries under demanding conditions proves the reactions between LiPSs and Li metal anodes are effectively impaired in HME- EPSE.

Li� S pouch cells with HME-EPSE Pouch cell is a favorable battery configuration to evaluate the feasibility of HME-EPSE in practical high-energydensity Li� S batteries.[4a] A Li� S pouch cell (2.7 Ah) was assembled with ultrathin Li anodes of 75 μm, high-arealloading S cathodes of 7.6 mgScm� 2 (on a single side), and an E/S ratio of 3.0 gelegS � 1 (Figure 4a).
The specific capacity of S cathode in the pouch cell is 1275 mAhg� 1 at 0.025 C.
The mass of each component in the Li� S pouch cell is presented in Figure 4b.
The total mass of the pouch cell is 14.92 g and the energy density is 387 Whkg� 1 (Figure 4c).
After 27 stable cycles, the Li� S pouch cell with HME-EPSE preserves a specific capacity of 748 mAhg� 1 with 58% retention and an energy density of 217 Whkg� 1 with 56% retention.

The charge� discharge profiles with typical two discharge plateaus are observed in Li� S pouch cells using HME-EPSE under lean electrolyte conditions, illustrating the wellmaintained S conversion kinetics in HME-EPSE (Figure 4d).
The performance of Li� S pouch cells with HME-EPSE is also compared with other regulation strategies (Figure S17 and Table S1).

The performance of Li� S pouch cells with HME-EPSE is balanced between cycle life and energy density compared with that using other regulation strategies, displaying the potential of HME-EPSE in practical Li� S batteries.
Compared with other EPSEs, HME-EPSE delivers a higher specific capacity at the same demanding conditions.
When the conditions of pouch cells are the same, the capacity of pouch cell with HME-EPSE is higher to achieve a higher energy density.

Therefore, owing to balancing the conversion reaction kinetics of the S cathodes and the protection of Li metal anodes, HME-EPSE endows Li� S pouch cells with both superior cycle life and high energy density.

Conclusion In conclusion, HME is proposed as a co-solvent to formulate EPSE so that the rate performance of S cathodes and the protection of Li metal anodes are balanced in Li� S batteries under practical conditions (Figure 5).
HME has a high reduction stability against Li metal anodes and weak solvating power to LiPSs.
Although the solvation structure of LiPSs in HME-EPSE resembles other EPSEs, the rate performance of Li� S batteries with HME-EPSE is superior.

Under practical conditions using an ultrathin Li metal anode (50 μm) and a high-loading S cathode (4.4 mgScm� 2), Li� S batteries with HME-EPSE exhibit a specific capacity of 1040 mAhg� 1 which is comparable with the cell with DOL/ DME electrolyte (1049 mAhg� 1) at 0.1 C.

Raw materials 1,3-dioxolane (DOL, battery grade, DoDoChem), 1,2- dimethoxyethane (DME, battery grade, DoDoChem), lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfony)imide (LiTFSI, battery grade, DoDoChem), lithium nitrate (LiNO3, metals basis, Aladdin), polypropylene (PP) separator (Celgard 2500), aluminum (Al) foil, lithium (Li) foil (50 or 75 μm thick), elemental sulfur (S), carbon nanotubes (CNTs), N-methyl-2- pyrrolidinone (NMP, Sinopharm), poly(vinylidene fluoride) (PVDF, HSV-300), and carbon paper (CP) were purchased from commercial sources and used without further purification.
Hexyl methyl ether (HME, 98%) was purchased from TCI (Shanghai) Development Co., Ltd. and purified by molecular sieve for over 24 h.
All the materials were kept in an argon-filled glove box (H2O < 0.1 ppm, O2 < 0.1 ppm). 2.
Preparation of sulfur cathodes A S/C composite was obtained from S and CNTs mixed by the weight ratio of 7:3.
Then, the S/C composite was ball-milled with PVDF binder (9:1, by wt.) in NMP.
After that, the slurry was cast onto aluminum (Al) foil and dried at 60°C for 12 h.
The S/C cathodes (S content = 63%) were cut into disks (φ =13.0 mm) before use.
The areal sulfur loading was controlled at 1.1, 4.4, or 9.9 mgS cm−2. 3.
Preparation of electrolytes The blank electrolyte was prepared with 1.0 M LiTFSI and 2.0 wt.% LiNO3 dissolved in DOL/DME (1:1, by vol.).
HME-EPSE was composed of 1.0 M LiTFSI and

Both electrolytes were prepared in an argon-filled glove box. 4.
Electrochemical measurement Under mild conditions, Li–S batteries were assembled with Li metal anodes (600 μm), regular-loading S cathodes (1.1 mgS cm−2), and 25 μL electrolyte.

Under demanding conditions, an ultrathin Li anode (50 μm), a high-loading S cathode (4.4 mgS cm−2) or an ultrahigh-loading S cathode (9.9 mgS cm−2), and electrolyte (35 or 90 μL, respectively) were employed to assemble Li–S batteries.
For batteries under demanding conditions, cycle performance was tested between 1.7–2.6 V at 0.1 C after 2 activation cycles at 0.05 C.
The rate performance of Li–S batteries was assessed at 0.1 C, 0.2 C, and 0.3 C.
The batteries were cycled for 5 cycles at each rate after 2 activation cycles at 0.05 C.

MD simulations MD simulations were conducted based on the Large Scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) code, and the OPLS-AA force field was

[3] The force field parameters for solvents were generated by the LigParGen web server except that advanced restrained electrostatic potential (RESP2) atomic partial charges were assigned to each atom, which were obtained based on electrostatic potential (ESP) charges using the Multiwfn program.[4] The parameters for Li+ and S82− were obtained from Jensen et al. and Rajput et al., respectively.[5] Two models with and without HME were constructed.
The model with HME contains 395 DOL, 265 DME, 18 Li2S8, and 122 HME molecules while the one without HME contains 516 DOL, 347 DME, and 18 Li2S8 molecules.

The initial atomic coordinates were generated with the Packing Optimization for Molecular Dynamics Simulations (Packmol) program.[6] The final solvation structures were visualized by VMD.[7] Each system was first equilibrated in the NPT ensemble for 2 ns to maintain a temperature of 298.15 K and a pressure of 1 atm with time constants of 0.1 and 1 ps, respectively.

Then, both systems were heated from 298.15 to 450.15 K within 0.5 ns, and maintained at 450.15 K for 1 ns, followed by annealing to 298.15 K within 0.5 ns and equilibrated in NPT ensemble for another 4 ns.
A production run of 7 ns was finally performed in NVT ensemble.
Only the final 5 ns trajectory was sampled for the analysis of solvation structures.
